name: Occipital lobe
func: The back part of each hemisphere and the brain's main vision center. It receives signals from the eyes via the thalamus and works out edges, colors, motion and shapes, with each side seeing the opposite half of the visual world.

levels.kid:
At the very back of your head, where your head touches the pillow, is your **occipital lobe**. It is your brain's **seeing** part.

Your eyes are like cameras. They take pictures and send them all the way to the back of your brain. The occipital lobe looks at the picture and figures out the colors, the lines, and what is moving.

Here is something surprising: your eyes are in the front, but seeing happens in the back!

If someone bumps the back of their head really hard, they might "see stars" for a moment. That is because the seeing part got shaken.
levels.hs:
The **occipital lobe** is the smallest lobe and forms the back of each hemisphere. It rests on the **tentorium cerebelli**, a sheet of tough dura that separates it from the cerebellum below. On the medial surface, the **parieto-occipital sulcus** separates it from the parietal lobe in front. On the outer surface there is no clear border.

The most important landmark is the **calcarine sulcus**, a deep groove on the medial surface running back toward the occipital pole. The **primary visual cortex (V1)** lines both banks of this sulcus. Above it is the **cuneus** ("wedge") and below it is the **lingual gyrus**.

Here is the key rule: each occipital lobe sees the **opposite half of the visual field** from both eyes. Signals from the retina travel along the optic nerves, partly cross at the **optic chiasm**, relay in the **lateral geniculate nucleus** of the thalamus and travel back through the **optic radiations** to V1. The upper bank of the calcarine sulcus represents the lower visual field, and the lower bank represents the upper field.

The center of vision, the **macula**, gets a large share of V1 at the occipital pole, because that is where we see fine detail, such as when reading. Areas around V1 (V2, V3, V4, V5) then process shape, color and motion.
levels.college:
V1 is **Brodmann area 17**, also called **striate cortex** because of the **stria of Gennari**, a white band of myelinated fibers in layer IV visible to the naked eye. Surrounding it are **BA 18 and 19**, the extrastriate visual areas.

**Retinotopy:** the visual field is mapped onto V1 with the fovea at the occipital pole and the periphery more anteriorly along the calcarine sulcus. Central vision is magnified (cortical magnification): the central few degrees occupy a large fraction of V1.

**Parallel pathways:** the **magnocellular** pathway (motion, low contrast, coarse detail) and **parvocellular** pathway (fine detail, red-green color) start in different retinal ganglion cells and LGN layers, and remain partly separate in V1. Beyond V1, signals split into the **dorsal stream** to parietal cortex ("where/how," including motion area **V5/MT** at the occipitotemporal junction) and the **ventral stream** to temporal cortex ("what," including color area **V4** on the fusiform/lingual region).

**Blood supply:** the **posterior cerebral artery** (via its calcarine branch) supplies V1. The occipital pole, where the macula is represented, also often receives a contribution from the **MCA**. This dual supply is the usual explanation for **macular sparing** in PCA strokes, though some authors suggest other factors, such as overlap in the cortical representation.

**Venous drainage** reaches the confluence of sinuses near the internal occipital protuberance, an important landmark for posterior fossa and occipital surgery.

The occipital lobe also contributes to eye movements, such as smooth pursuit and fixation, through connections with the parietal and frontal eye fields and the superior colliculus.
levels.phd:
Hubel and Wiesel (Nobel Prize 1981) found that V1 neurons respond best to **oriented edges**. **Simple cells** have elongated receptive fields with distinct on and off zones, while **complex cells** respond to an edge of the right orientation anywhere within a larger field. V1 is organized into **orientation columns**, **ocular dominance columns** (alternating left-eye and right-eye input in layer IV) and **cytochrome oxidase blobs** rich in color-selective cells, together forming repeating **hypercolumns** that cover each point of the visual field. In living cortex, orientation preference forms pinwheels around singular points.

**Critical periods:** Hubel and Wiesel showed that closing one eye in kittens during early life shifted ocular dominance columns toward the open eye and caused lasting vision loss in the closed eye. This is the basis of **amblyopia** ("lazy eye") in children, which is why it is treated early with patching or blurring the stronger eye. The closure of critical periods involves maturation of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons and the formation of perineuronal nets, and research is exploring ways to reopen plasticity in adults.

**Predictive coding** models propose that higher visual areas send predictions back to V1, and V1 signals the mismatch. Feedback connections from higher areas outnumber feedforward ones in many cortical circuits.

**Blindsight:** some people with V1 damage can point to or discriminate stimuli in their blind field above chance while denying they see anything (Weiskrantz). This is thought to rely on pathways that bypass V1, such as from the LGN or superior colliculus via the pulvinar directly to extrastriate areas like MT.

**Cross-modal plasticity:** in people blind from early life, the occipital cortex is recruited for Braille reading and auditory tasks.
levels.expert:
**Visual field defects** localize lesions along the visual pathway:

- A **PCA stroke** typically causes a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia**, often with **macular sparing**. Patients may bump into things on the blind side without realizing why.
- A lesion of one bank of the calcarine sulcus gives a **homonymous quadrantanopia**: the upper bank (cuneus) causes an inferior defect, the lower bank (lingual gyrus) a superior defect.
- Occipital pole damage causes central **homonymous scotomas**.
- **Bilateral occipital infarction** (for example from a basilar artery "top of the basilar" embolus) gives **cortical blindness**. Pupils still react to light, because the reflex bypasses the cortex. In **Anton syndrome**, the patient denies being blind and confabulates descriptions.

**Higher visual disorders:** **achromatopsia** (loss of color vision from V4 damage), **akinetopsia** (inability to see motion, from bilateral V5 damage), and **alexia without agraphia**, from a left PCA stroke damaging the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum: the patient can write but cannot read what they wrote.

**Occipital seizures** cause flashing lights or colored shapes in the opposite visual field. **Migraine aura** is often a slowly spreading zigzag (fortification spectrum), thought to reflect **cortical spreading depression** moving across visual cortex at a few millimeters per minute.

**Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)** shows symmetric parieto-occipital edema on MRI, often linked to very high blood pressure or certain medicines, and usually reverses with treatment of the cause.

**Imaging:** MRI with DWI for stroke; CT angiography to look at the PCA and basilar artery.

**Surgery:** occipital approaches (for example the **occipital transtentorial approach**) reach the pineal region. Surgeons use visual field testing before and after and tractography of the optic radiations to limit field loss.

keyPoints: Back of the brain, resting on the tentorium cerebelli
V1 = BA 17 (striate cortex) lining the calcarine sulcus
Each lobe sees the opposite visual field of both eyes
PCA stroke → contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Bilateral damage → cortical blindness; Anton syndrome = denial

test.q: The primary visual cortex lines which sulcus?
test.explain: V1 sits on both banks of the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface.

test.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays vision to the occipital lobe? (abbreviation or full name)
test.explain: Retinal axons synapse in the LGN, which projects via the optic radiations to V1.

test.q: A left PCA stroke causes which visual field defect?
choices: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Blindness in the left eye only
test.explain: The left occipital lobe sees the right visual field; macular sparing is common.

test.q: V1 is called striate cortex because of:
test.explain: The stria of Gennari is a band of myelinated fibers in layer IV.

test.q: A cortically blind patient who insists they can see has ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Anton syndrome follows bilateral occipital damage.

test.q: Who discovered orientation-selective simple and complex cells in V1?
test.explain: Hubel and Wiesel won the 1981 Nobel Prize for this work.
